name: Loose Larry
description: Loose Larry plays way too many hands and almost never folds once he puts money in the pot. He loves seeing flops with any two cards and will call down with bottom pair, gutshots, and even ace-high. He rarely raises or 3-bets, preferring to passively call and hope to hit. His high VPIP (52%) and low PFR (8%) reveal a massive gap -- he enters pots but almost never with aggression. His went-to-showdown (42%) is extremely high, confirming he takes weak hands to the river far too often.
strategyExplanation: Against Loose Larry, your primary adjustment is to value bet relentlessly and avoid bluffing. Since he calls with a wide range of weak hands, every value bet you make prints money. Bet three streets with top pair decent kicker or better. Size your bets larger than normal (60-75% pot) since he is not price-sensitive and will call regardless. Eliminate bluffs and semi-bluffs from your range -- he will call you down and you will lose money with air. Thin value bets become very profitable: hands like second pair or weak top pair that you would normally check can be bet for value. Do not try to push him off hands with big bets; instead, let him call you off with worse.

name: Nervous Nate
description: Nervous Nate only plays premium hands and folds everything else. His extremely tight VPIP of 12% means he enters roughly 1 in 8 hands, and when he does, he usually raises (PFR of 10% is close to his VPIP, showing a tight-aggressive preflop style). However, his postflop play is predictable and fearful. His fold-to-3-bet of 85% is exploitably high, and his low went-to-showdown (24%) shows he gives up easily when facing resistance. When he does bet or raise postflop, he almost always has a strong hand.
strategyExplanation: Exploit Nervous Nate by stealing his blinds relentlessly and 3-betting him light. His 85% fold-to-3-bet means you profit by 3-betting him with any two cards when he opens. When he calls your 3-bet or 4-bets, you must respect his range and tighten up dramatically. Postflop, c-bet at a high frequency because he folds too much without a strong hand. If he raises your c-bet or leads into you, alarm bells should ring -- fold anything less than a very strong hand. His low WTSD means you can barrel him off medium-strength hands on the turn and river. The key is to be aggressive when he shows weakness and get out of the way fast when he shows strength.

name: Maniac Mike
description: Maniac Mike is a hyper-aggressive player who raises and re-raises with an extremely wide range. His 62% VPIP and 40% PFR show he enters most pots with a raise, applying constant pressure. His aggression factor of 4.2 is off the charts, meaning he bets and raises far more often than he calls. He 3-bets 14% of the time, which includes many bluffs and speculative hands. His c-bet frequency of 80% means he fires at nearly every flop regardless of his hand. He thrives on making opponents uncomfortable and forcing folds.
bestStrategy: Trap and Let Him Hang Himself
strategyExplanation: The biggest mistake against Maniac Mike is trying to outbluff him or fight fire with fire. Instead, widen your calling range preflop with hands that play well postflop (suited connectors, suited aces, broadway hands). Call his 3-bets more often with hands like AJ, KQ, TT-JJ instead of folding. Postflop, let him barrel into you by check-calling with medium and strong hands rather than raising, which lets him continue bluffing on multiple streets. Set traps by checking strong hands and letting him bet. When you do raise, make it large because he may still call with a wide range. Tighten your opening range slightly since he will 3-bet you frequently, but do not over-fold to his aggression -- he is bluffing far too often to justify folding strong top pair or overpairs.

name: Tactical Tom
description: Tactical Tom is a tight-aggressive (TAG) regular who plays a disciplined, fundamentally sound game. His 22% VPIP and 18% PFR indicate he selects strong starting hands and usually enters pots with a raise. His aggression factor of 2.8 is well-balanced, showing he bets for value and bluffs at appropriate frequencies. His 3-bet of 7% is a solid mix of value and bluffs, and his fold-to-3-bet of 60% shows he does not over-defend. This is the type of player you will encounter most often at mid-stakes and above.
strategyExplanation: Against Tactical Tom, there are no massive exploits -- you need to play solid, position-aware poker. Focus on having position on him whenever possible; his range is tighter out of position. 3-bet him occasionally with suited connectors and suited aces to keep him honest, targeting his 60% fold-to-3-bet. Postflop, do not try to bluff him on boards that favor his range (dry, high-card boards). Instead, look for spots on dynamic boards where he may check-fold marginal hands. He is harder to extract value from since he folds appropriately, so mix in some smaller sizings with your value hands to keep him calling. Float his c-bets in position on wet boards since his 65% c-bet frequency means he has air about a third of the time.

name: Aggressive Anna
description: Aggressive Anna is a loose-aggressive (LAG) player who combines a wider-than-average starting hand range with strong postflop aggression. Her 30% VPIP and 24% PFR show she plays many hands but almost always with a raise. Her aggression factor of 3.5 indicates she applies significant postflop pressure with bets and raises. Unlike a maniac, Anna is selective about her aggression -- she picks good spots to bluff and size her bets well. Her 10% 3-bet includes both value hands and well-chosen bluffs. She is one of the tougher player types to play against.
strategyExplanation: Playing against Aggressive Anna requires strong hand reading skills. Since her range is wider than a TAG but she plays skillfully, you need to identify when she is strong versus bluffing. Defend wider against her opens and 3-bets since her range is looser, but be prepared for postflop battles. Use position aggressively -- call her raises in position with suited hands and pocket pairs to leverage postflop skill. When she c-bets frequently, float in position with overcards and backdoor draws, then take the pot away on the turn when she checks. Do not slow-play strong hands -- she will control the pot with checks when you trap. Instead, build pots by betting and raising your strong hands, since she is capable of calling with wider ranges than a nit. Be willing to make big folds when her betting pattern shifts to very large sizings on the river.

name: Fishy Frank
description: Fishy Frank is a recreational player with no coherent strategy. His 45% VPIP and 12% PFR show he limps into many pots but rarely raises, indicating a passive preflop approach. His aggression factor of 1.0 means he calls as often as he bets or raises, showing no clear betting strategy. His 3-bet of 3% is almost exclusively premium hands, meaning his rare raises are very strong. His c-bet of 45% is inconsistent -- sometimes he bets, sometimes he does not, with no clear pattern. He makes many fundamental errors including playing too many hands, calling too much, and misvaluing hand strength.
strategyExplanation: Against Fishy Frank, keep your strategy simple and straightforward. Isolate him preflop by raising over his limps with a wide range of hands that have equity (suited hands, broadway cards, pairs). This gets you heads-up in position against a weak player. Postflop, play ABC poker: bet your strong hands for value, check your weak hands, and bluff only on very favorable board textures where his range is weak. Since his aggression factor is 1.0, when he does bet or raise, he usually has something -- respect his rare aggression. Do not try fancy plays like check-raises or multi-street bluffs; he will not understand what you are representing and will call anyway. Size your value bets around 50-66% pot to keep him calling with his wide range. The goal is to play a high volume of straightforward, profitable pots.
